item.title: Your Best Ideas Are Waiting Outside
item.description:
Creativity

Your Best Ideas Are Waiting Outside

The most powerful thinking tool you own isn't in your pocket. It's in your shoes.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI is dazzlingly fast. But some of your best ideas arrive at walking pace, about three miles an hour.
  • A Stanford study found that walking boosts creative idea generation by an average of 60 percent.
  • The same Stanford study found the boost lasts, even after you sit back down.
  • Beethoven, Woolf, Thoreau, and Darwin didn't walk instead of working. Walking was the work.
Source: cartoon by author Lisa Rothstein

I'm writing this sentence at my desk. And I can already feel it starting. The fidgeting. The reflexive reach for my phone. The sudden, urgent conviction that this is the perfect moment to declutter my art supply collection or catch up (months late) on my spring cleaning.

My desk is where the creative work is supposed to happen. So why does my brain treat it like a grindstone?

If you've ever stared down a blinking cursor, willing a good idea to emerge in the time block you so carefully and responsibly inserted in your calendar, only to have one fall from the sky when you were walking the dog, you already know the secret.

Your best thinking rarely happens where you planned for it to. It happens when your body is moving.

Here's why that's worth noticing (and harnessing) right now.

What Speed Can't Buy

Artificial intelligence is astonishingly fast. Ask it a question and the answer simply appears, fully formed, before you've finished your coffee, or even mid-first-sip. No waiting, no staring into space, no wandering off mid-thought.

And for a huge range of work, that speed is a genuine gift. I lean on it all the time, sometimes while I'm out walking and talking to it on my phone. But while it’s great for organizing activities or planning a project, or for tedium like writing a proposal, speed isn't the same as insight. Some of the best ideas can't be summoned on demand. They manifest in their own time, and that time (for me, and, it turns out, for many of history’s great thinkers) tends to move at about three miles an hour.

What Stanford Found on a Treadmill

The most original human thinking has never been a matter of speed. In 2014, Stanford researchers Marily Oppezzo and Daniel Schwartz ran a beautifully simple experiment. They measured people's creativity while sitting versus while walking. Walking increased creative output by a whopping 60 percent on average. And, most encouraging, the boost didn't evaporate the moment the subjects sat back down. It kept going even after they returned to their desks.

They titled the paper "Give Your Ideas Some Legs." (I wish I’d thought of that.)

There's a crucial detail in the fine print: walking supercharged divergent thinking, the freewheeling generation of brainstorms and new possibilities, not convergent thinking, the more narrow, judgmental kind we use when editing or finalizing something.

In other words, walking boosts exactly the kind of thinking that's the most satisfying to do ourselves, rather than handing it over to technology.

The Original Walking Thinkers

The great minds knew this in their bodies long before anyone measured it.

Beethoven took a long walk every afternoon and carried paper and a pencil, in case a melody caught up with him. Virginia Woolf recited her sentences aloud as she walked, and called a solo walk through London "the greatest rest." Henry David Thoreau probably put it most clearly: "Methinks that the moment my legs begin to move, my thoughts begin to flow."

Charles Darwin wore a literal path into the earth: a gravel loop near his home that he walked three times a day, kicking stones as he turned over the idea that became his theory of evolution. Friedrich Nietzsche went further, insisting that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking.

They didn't walk instead of working. The walking itself was the work.

51 Breeds and a Phone Full of Ideas

I saw this play out for myself last month in New York. Every morning I walked in Central Park, and every morning it was the best part of my day.

Partly because of the dogs.

I'm an unapologetic dog-breed nerd, so I started keeping a running tally; by the last morning, I'd counted 51 different breeds, not including duplicates. (Central Park, for reasons I have yet to crack, runs heavily to Cavalier King Charles spaniels and Australian shepherds.) That list grew right alongside another one: the cartoon premises and column hooks I kept stopping to dictate into my phone before they could float away.

Chained to my desk, that same hour would have felt like galley slavery. Out in the park, it was pure pleasure. (I also came home to San Diego a few weeks later two pounds lighter, which my desk has never once managed to do for me.)

Leaving the Monsters at the Desk

I think I know why it works, and it's not only the blood flow to the brain.

When I sit at my desk, I'm surrounded by my own gaggle of little monsters: distraction, resistance, procrastination, self-doubt, guilt, and the merciless blank page, staring back. They are very, very good at their jobs.

The moment I stand up and start moving, I’m able to leave them behind. It’s as if they can't keep up. That’s when the good stuff finally floats to the surface: connections, clarity, humor, the odd sideways idea I'd never have reached by force or self-flagellation. Plus, I get my steps in.

Source: sketch by author Lisa Rothstein

No Algorithm Has Legs

This is where it connects to what I keep calling Proof of Humanity.

A machine can generate a thousand ideas in the time it takes you to tie your shoes. What it can't do is be the body that gets restless, steps outside, and lets an answer surface at walking pace. That restlessness isn't a bug to be squashed. It's the feature. It's the part of us that produced the symphonies, the novels, and the theories we still read, hear, and celebrate a century or two later.

One caution, because I've sabotaged plenty of good walks this way: leave the earbuds at home. You can’t create when you’re consuming. The walk works precisely because nothing is filling the space: no podcast, no call, no feed. The boredom is the point. That's the room where ideas flow in.

So use the machine for what it's brilliant at. And then, when you're truly stuck, or when you simply want the pleasure of working something out for yourself, stand up. Leave your monsters at the desk. Take the most powerful thinking tool you own out for a walk.

Let the machine have instantaneous. I’ll take three miles an hour.

item.title: Why Is My Child Still Refusing to See Me Five Years After Divorce?
item.description:
Divorce

Why Is My Child Still Refusing to See Me Five Years After Divorce?

Apology can help heal ruptured attachment bonds that arise during gray divorce.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Gray divorce often deeply wounds children of all ages.
  • A ruptured parent-child attachment bond can cause a child's refusal to see a parent after divorce.
  • Meaningful and effective apologies can facilitate healing for estranged parents and their children.

Gray divorce refers to couples 50 and older ending their marriage. Currently, 36 percent of U.S. adults divorcing are 50 or older, and many have minor children.

Jerrod sad and cupping his head in his hands
Source: Kindelmedia / Pexels

Sitting across from me in my office, Jerrod, 55, cupped his head in his hands as his words slowly emerged. "It's been almost six years since I told her mom I wanted a divorce. Madeline was 14. She's almost 20 now and still refuses to see me or communicate with me by text, email, or phone call."

My therapy dog, Friede, offered her nose to his hands in comfort. He raised his head and began to scratch the soft fur on her head and ears. Looking at her through his teary eyes with a tense smile, he said, "Thanks for your support, Friede."

He invited Friede to join him on the loveseat and continued. "I keep replaying everything she said to me before I moved out of our home, like, 'You're a hypocrite. You always taught me how important it was to have virtues like honesty, loyalty, and trustworthiness. You have none of those!'"

He paused and fell silent for a moment. "She screamed at me, 'You have destroyed our family. You're destroying my freshman year in high school! I can never get his time back! And, you've been having an affair with my soccer coach! How could you?! I'm devastated and embarrassed! What if my friends and their parents find out? You have betrayed my mom and me. You only care about yourself!'

"She was right back then. I was not a good father to her. I hurt her in so many ways. You know how much I've worked on healing myself. Her mom and I have finally finished the divorce. I want to be the better father she needs, but she won't give me the chance to show her how much I have changed."

"Jerrod, we've talked about how the divorce is a crisis for all three of you. What Madeline experienced ruptured the strong bond that you and she had throughout the years. You probably recall that Madeline, her mom, and you signed a release allowing Dr. Benson, Madeline's individual therapist, and me to talk. Recently, she and I discussed that she thinks Madeline is ready to receive an apology letter from you that you and I will work on together, and I will email it to Dr. Benson for her to read with Madeline."

article continues after advertisement

"That's wonderful! What should I say in that letter?"

"That's a good question. Here's a handout I've written that describes the elements of a meaningful apology and how it can heal. Are you willing to read it with me now and discuss it, so I can help you with the wording and understanding?"

"Absolutely!" Jerrod's face glowed with hope.

Jerrod and I read and discussed the following in the handout.

What Are the Elements of a Meaningful Apology?

Different authors use different words to capture the elements of a meaningful apology. Essentially, they include:

  1. Acknowledge the action (what you did) with specificity.

2. Acknowledge what line was crossed (the transgression).

3. Acknowledge the adverse impact/consequences of the action and the hurt it caused.

4. Express sorrow, remorse, shame, and humility sincerely.

5. Pledge to alter future behavior.

6. Offer restitution, if appropriate, for example, a gift, an honor, or a financial exchange, if appropriate.

7. Avoid “if, but, maybe.”

8. Ask for forgiveness, if appropriate and without pressuring, for example, “I hope you can forgive me, and I understand if you’re not ready.”

Meaningful and Effective Apologies Can Help Healing by:

  1. Affirming that both people have shared values
  2. Agreeing that the harm committed was wrong
  3. Acknowledging that the victim was not responsible for the injury
  4. Providing assurance that the injured person is safe from a repeat offense

"After reading this, I can understand why people don't know what a meaningful apology is."

"You are right, Jerrod. Most people don't know what to include to make their apology meaningful and effective and how they can help heal their relationships.

"For our next session, are you willing to use this handout, reflect on and write your comments about all the points you think relate to your relationship with Madeline, write your meaningful and effective apology, and email it to me, so I can review it before we meet?"

article continues after advertisement

"Yes, I'm excited to do it and see you and Friede next session."

item.title: Can Contemporary Psychotherapy Be Blamed for Our Societal Ills?
item.description:
Therapy

Can Contemporary Psychotherapy Be Blamed for Our Societal Ills?

How much influence, pro or con, does psychotherapy truly exert on society today?

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Critics argue "therapy culture" fosters societal division and personal dependency.
  • Psychotherapy reflects societal values more than it shapes them.
  • Psychotherapy can't transform society, but can empower individuals to influence it.

This post is Part 2 of a series.

Source: Timur Weber / Pexels

According to philosopher and social critic Christina Hoff Sommers (One Nation Under Therapy, 2005) and author and licensed mental health counselor Jonathan Alpert (Therapy Nation, 2026), what Alpert disapprovingly calls our current "therapy culture" and Sommers deems "therapism" contribute heavily to the problems polarizing, dividing, and disintegrating American society today, diminishes our mental health promoting dependency and weakness rather than resilience and independence (see Part 1), "has reshaped the way we live, speak, and relate to one another...[and] is changing the fabric of American life." Quite an indictment! But this begs the big question: How much influence, pro or con, does the practice of psychotherapy truly exert on society today? Is the profession of psychotherapy really so extraordinarily powerful?

Indeed, from a very different perspective (such as mine), which considers psychotherapy a precious and still vitally important process promoting personal responsibility, freedom, consciousness, compassion, creativity, balance, vitality, and wholeness, or what Jung termed individuation, it would be wonderful to believe that the practice of psychotherapy could be so profoundly impactful on American culture—one way or the other. But, sadly, the reality is that this simply has not been the case, as somewhat pessimistically noted in an earlier book titled We've Had a Hundred Years of Psychotherapy--And the World's Getting Worse by James Hillman and Michael Ventura (1993).

Psychotherapy and American Culture

It is true that psychotherapy has become more popular, accessible, and ubiquitous today than ever before. But has it truly infiltrated American culture as pervasively as these authors suggest? Yes, certainly since its turn-of-the-20th-century inception, Freud's psychoanalysis, the first systematized form of psychotherapy, permeated Western culture in particular with popular new concepts and terminology such as "the unconscious," "Oedipal complex," "free association," "neurosis," etc., much as some of the diagnostic language of today's psychotherapies—"trauma," "narcissism," "psychopath," "borderline personality," "bipolar disorder," "OCD," "PTSD," "ADHD," etc.—have inevitably seeped into our daily lexicon, sometimes losing their true meaning or clinical significance. However, while engaging in what has pejoratively been referred to as "psychobabble" or "therapy-speak" on the part of the public may be unavoidable, psychotherapy cannot be held responsible for such ignorance, superficiality, or misuse of technical terms. What this does demonstrate is the public's insatiable curiosity about therapy and the need for such psychological concepts and language in their daily lives.

Whereas Sommers and Alpert see psychotherapy itself as the insidious source of some of today's most concerning social ills, such as self-absorption and victim mentality, I submit it is society that influences psychotherapy and those who provide it more than the other way around. Psychotherapy reflects or mirrors the values, beliefs, and problems of the culture in which it is rooted rather than vice versa. Psychotherapy is, has always been, and will always be an integral part of the culture from which it springs. But, at its best, it also provides patients with some constructive alternative to the culture's conventional wisdom or worldview and the freedom, support, and encouragement to be true to one's self despite considerable societal pressures to conform. Psychotherapy is not simply about learning to adjust oneself to one's family and society but sometimes entails encouraging the individual's need to take a stand against unfair or destructive familial or societal norms, practices, and prejudices.

From my own perspective, based on five decades as a practicing psychotherapist here in California, while I still consider psychotherapy to be a potentially helpful and sometimes transformative process for individuals, couples, or families, I no longer believe that it can or will radically transform society per se. But this is not to say that the individual who has been positively transformed by psychotherapy cannot and does not influence the collective culture in constructive or creative ways. (I am thinking, for example, of someone like Bruce Springsteen and many other artists who have benefitted from therapy.) The same may be said of those people who have had negative experiences with psychotherapy. But it in no way negates the value, relevance, and importance of psychotherapy and its burgeoning necessity in our day.

Psychotherapy Amid Social and Global Turmoil

Indeed, now, more than ever, we need the encouragement, insight, and inspiration that the previous century of cumulative clinical wisdom of psychotherapy can provide. As Jung (1961) himself succinctly stated, "Today we need psychology [and psychotherapy] for reasons that involve our very existence." His words ring doubly true in these deeply unsettling, tense, and troubled times. Are people more anxious and depressed these days? This is a statistically supported fact. But is it due to the pervasive influence and failures of psychotherapy? Here in America, a highly polarized and increasingly violent conflict between left and right, liberal and conservative, Republican and Democrat, threatens the once unthinkable possibility of a second civil war. A seemingly inevitable global clash between radical Islam and Judeo-Christian or secular Western culture rages on, each side perceiving the other as evil incarnate. And, like some proverbial Sword of Damocles dangling dangerously over our heads by a thread, the very real and horrifying possibility of imminent nuclear war with North Korea, China, or Russia threatens global annihilation. The future of civilization—and each one of us—hangs precariously in the balance. How could someone not feel more anxious or depressed?

But this does not take therapy totally off the hook. Its inability and refusal to deal more constructively and deeply with people's anxiety, despair, grief, anger, or rage and overreliance on potent psychiatric medications to manage and suppress these daimonic emotions can be iatrogenic, making matters even worse for those seeking psychological assistance. (See Diamond, 1996.) Nonetheless, despite dubious trends in recent decades toward a more superficial neurobiological, pharmacological, and cognitive-behavioral approach to the understanding and treatment of psychiatric disorders, there remains a profound, pervasive, and palpable personal and collective hunger for real, in-depth psychological, philosophical, and spiritual guidance, knowledge, and clinical wisdom. This is the extremely challenging and essential task of psychotherapy today. (See Part 3.)

item.title: The Overlooked Happiness of Anticipation
item.description:
Happiness

The Overlooked Happiness of Anticipation

How looking forward can make you happier.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Savoring includes enjoying positive experiences before, during, and after they occur.
  • Anticipating rewarding events can generate positive emotions in advance.
  • Creating things to look forward to may increase positive affectivity over time.

I’ve been in Japan for the past few weeks teaching a study-abroad course called “The Science of Happiness.” It’s been an amazing trip, but I’ve been starting to miss my family and the comforts of home.

Last night, I started imagining sleeping in my own bed, cuddling with my kids, and ordering a pizza from our favorite place. I started to feel my mood lift as I anticipated my first couple days at home.

Most of us think happiness comes from experiences themselves. But positive psychology suggests that we can start reaping the benefits of positive experiences long before they happen.

In fact, anticipation may be one of the easiest ways to lift your mood.

What Is Savoring?

Positive psychology examines how people can increase positive emotions such as joy, gratitude, contentment, and excitement.

One of the most effective ways to do this is through a practice called savoring.

Savoring involves prolonging and enhancing positive experiences so that you get more emotional benefit from them. For example, enjoying a delicious meal is even more pleasurable when you’re not scrolling on your phone while you eat it.

There are three types of savoring:

  1. Savoring the present: This means fully appreciating a positive experience while it is happening. This could look like watching a beautiful sunset or even taking a moment to bask in a big accomplishment, rather than immediately moving on to the next task.

  2. Reminiscing on positive memories and re-experiencing some of the associated emotions: For example, every year, on the anniversary of the day I met my husband, I imagine the events of that night in great detail. It never fails to bring me joy.

  3. Anticipating something enjoyable that has not happened yet: This could be an upcoming vacation or achieving a milestone you’ve been working toward.

Anticipation and Positive Affectivity

In personality psychology, the tendency to experience positive emotions is called positive affectivity. This trait reflects how readily we experience emotions such as enthusiasm, excitement, and joy.

Psychologists used to believe that personality traits like positive affectivity were largely fixed. Today, we know they are more malleable than previously thought.

One way people increase positive affectivity is by intentionally engaging in activities that generate positive emotions. Anticipatory savoring is one such activity.

When you regularly give yourself things to look forward to and allow yourself to enjoy the anticipation, you create more opportunities to experience positive emotions. Over time, these experiences can reinforce the tendency to notice rewards, seek enjoyment, and approach life with greater enthusiasm.

In other words, what begins as a moment of happiness habit may gradually become part of your personality.

A Simple Happiness Intervention

One of the easiest ways to increase positive affect is to make sure you always have something you're looking forward to. It doesn't have to be expensive or elaborate. For example:

  • A walk with a friend.
  • Trying a new coffee shop.
  • A Friday movie night.
  • A phone call with someone you miss.
  • A Saturday morning spent reading a novel.

The period of anticipation gives us an opportunity to experience joy before the event arrives. So if you'd like to feel a little happier this week, ask yourself: What is one thing I can put on my calendar that I'll genuinely look forward to?

item.title: How to Have the Right Mindset—Free of Judgment—When Traveling
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

How to Have the Right Mindset—Free of Judgment—When Traveling

Is criticism bad for your mental health when you travel?

Posted June 29, 2026

One of the most exciting parts of life is having the good fortune of traveling to different countries and cultures. Even so, some people can be critical of other countries.

For example, when I was in a van in Turkey, I was gushing with enthusiasm about the country. Behind me, two women were discussing why they didn’t like Turkey. “What kind of country is this?” one of them said. “They don’t even speak English and expect us to speak Turkish. And can’t even get a good piña colada here. At home, they have them everywhere.”

In Brazil, I heard a religious leader speak very frankly to a group of complaining tourists when he said, “If you want to get along with Brazilian people, don’t criticize their country.”

In the U.S., visitors from abroad sometimes vent about Americans speaking too loudly or obsessing about money or wanting them to tip if someone hands them an ice cream cone.

In China, travelers I met were appalled by squat toilets and refused to use them. In Paris, visitors complained that locals were condescending if they didn’t speak French.

I contacted a cross-cultural expert about how our mental health is affected when we are judgmental and critical about places and customs we encounter when traveling, and whether there is a psychological downside to comparing them unfavorably to what we already know.

Craig Storti, who helms an intercultural training business and is the author of 10 books about cultural differences, had this to say:

“The whole point of travel is to experience something new and different and thereby add to your sensibility, and deepen/expand your perspective. If you’re thinking about/missing home all the time, you don’t learn very much. If you don’t come home changed, you’ve missed a great opportunity to add to who you are. Another reason it’s silly to compare abroad unfavorably with home is that it prevents you from seeing home from a new perspective and learning therefrom. It has often been said that the true value of foreign travel is to more clearly see and thus better understand the place you come from, and thus in the end to better understand yourself.”

I asked him why people from the U.S. expect others to speak English.

“There’s a saying in my field,” he replied. “Someone who is trilingual speaks three languages; someone who is bilingual speaks two languages, and someone who is monolingual comes from the United States. You can travel three thousand miles, the length and breadth of America, and never encounter someone who doesn’t speak English. And we get used to that. Also, since American culture—well, music and movies, anyway—are known throughout the world, we think everybody must also know our language.”

From my own experience, many travelers won’t even consider going to a country where people don’t speak English. Language anxiety (or xenoglossophobia) is the term for the feeling of nervousness and worry people may have when they are learning another language, or trying to speak a second language.

Preply, an online education platform that specializes in teaching languages, conducted a survey of over 1,500 U.S. adults. It focused on travel anxiety and revealed that while 39% planned to go abroad, nearly a third (32%) intentionally chose destinations where English is widely spoken. According to a Preply blog post, “this could mean Americans are limiting themselves to more familiar experiences, and missing the chance to connect more deeply with the places they visit."

As a travel journalist, I often recommend learning a phrase or even words like “hello” and “thank you” in the language of the country you are traveling to. It’s not just about language—it’s a way to show locals that you are interested in them, in communicating with them, and in experiencing their culture. And it also makes you feel more confident and proud of yourself when you connect with locals.

I also asked Storti what he thinks is a mentally healthy way to experience other cultures and countries.

“To observe without judging. To avoid your countrymen and women when you travel. To get outside your comfort zone and have the humbling experience of being a fool and not understanding what’s going on around you. Uncomfortable experiences are a very good way to grow. We don’t learn from experiencing the familiar; we learn from encountering what is different. Don’t be afraid to make a fool of yourself,” he said.

Bon voyage, and may you leave all that you know at home when you embark on a trip and are open to learning more about the destination and yourself. And, from personal experience, sometimes the most awkward, strange, or uncomfortable situations make the best stories when you return home.

item.title: Summer Can Be Hard on Body Image
item.description:
Body Image

Summer Can Be Hard on Body Image

5 ways to challenge appearance anxiety and self-criticism.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Body image often shapes attention more than appearance itself.
  • Confidence grows from self-worth, not from achieving a particular body size.
  • Avoiding meaningful experiences tends to strengthen, not resolve, body image concerns.

Summer has a way of amplifying negative body image. More of the body is visible, social calendars fill up, and activities like swimming, traveling, and attending outdoor events can leave people feeling exposed in ways they don't during other times of the year.

Source: Warren Umoh / Unsplash

It's easy to assume that the distress comes from the body itself. Yet in my work as a therapist specializing in the treatment of eating disorders and body image distress, I often find that the deeper struggle is not about appearance but about attention. Body image concerns can quietly consume mental and emotional energy, pulling people away from the experiences they value most. Instead of being present with friends, family, or meaningful activities, they become preoccupied with how they look, how much space they take up, or how they compare to others.

If summer has become another season spent evaluating your body, it may be worth considering a different approach.

1. Notice Where Your Attention Goes

Body image struggles often operate in the background. You might catch yourself checking your reflection in a store window, adjusting your shirt before walking into a room, comparing your body to someone else's at the pool, or replaying a conversation while wondering how you looked the entire time. These moments can become so automatic that you barely notice they're happening.

The goal is not to eliminate body-critical thoughts. Most people can't simply decide to stop having them. Instead, start by noticing when they show up. You might silently label them by saying to yourself, "There's my body critic," or "I'm having the thought that my body isn't good enough." Naming the thought creates a little distance between you and it.

From there, see if you can gently shift your attention back to the present moment. You might notice the warmth of the sun on your skin, the sound of someone laughing nearby, the feeling of your feet on the ground, or the taste of the food you're eating.

It may also help to remember that these thoughts often develop as a form of protection. Your mind may believe that if it criticizes you first, it can shield you from rejection or judgment by others. Ironically, that strategy often keeps the cycle of self-judgment going. You don't have to argue with the thought or convince yourself it's untrue. You can simply acknowledge it, thank your mind for trying to protect you, and return your attention to the life unfolding around you.

2. Question the Authority of Body-Critical Thoughts

When a thought is repeated often enough, it can start to feel like a fact. Over time, statements such as "Everyone is noticing my body" or "I look terrible today" may become so familiar that they go unchallenged. Yet body image is determined by far more than objective reality. Mood, stress, past experiences, cultural messages, and even a poor night's sleep can influence how someone perceives their appearance.

Rather than arguing with every negative thought, it may be more useful to approach them with curiosity. What evidence supports this belief? What evidence might contradict it? If a friend spoke about themselves this way, would you automatically assume they were correct? These questions do not eliminate body dissatisfaction, but they can loosen its grip.

3. Consider What Body Dissatisfaction Is Costing You

People often focus on what body dissatisfaction is trying to do for them. They hope it will motivate change, protect them from judgment, or keep them from becoming complacent. Less attention is given to what it takes away.

Over the years, I've heard people describe postponing vacations, avoiding photographs, declining invitations, putting off dating, delaying clothing purchases, and withdrawing from activities they genuinely wanted to experience. In each case, the hope was that life would feel easier once the body changed.

Sometimes the body changes, and the anxiety remains. The standards simply shift, and a new concern takes the place of the old one. Thinking about what body dissatisfaction has cost you can be uncomfortable, but it can also clarify whether continuing to follow its rules is getting you where you want to go.

4. Let Your Values Carry More Weight Than Appearance Concerns

Body image often encourages avoidance. It tells people to stay home, cover up, sit out, or wait until they feel more confident. While avoidance can deliver temporary relief, it tends to reinforce the idea that appearance concerns are dangerous or demand special accommodation.

Values offer a different compass. Rather than asking, "How do I feel about my body today?" it can be helpful to ask, "What matters to me in this moment?"The answer may be connected with family, time with friends, creativity, adventure, relaxation, advocacy, spirituality, or simply being present. Making decisions based on those values does not require body confidence. It requires a willingness to give precedence to what matters over what appearance anxiety demands.

5. Stop Waiting for a Future Version of Yourself

Source: AllGo - An App For Plus Size People / Unsplash

Many people carry the belief that confidence will arrive once they lose weight, fit into a certain clothing size, or finally feel good about what they see in the mirror. They imagine that a different body will allow them to relax, participate more fully, and stop worrying about what other people think.

The problem is that confidence built on appearance is inherently fragile. If your confidence depends on liking your body every day, fitting into a particular size, or believing you measure up to those around you, it can disappear the moment those conditions change.

Body confidence is something different. It's the ability to move through the world knowing that your worth is not determined by your appearance. It's trusting that if you need to buy the larger size, if your body changes over time, or if you happen to be the largest person in the room, those facts do not make you less interesting, less capable, less lovable, or less deserving of belonging.

That doesn't mean you have to love every part of your body. Most people don't. It means your relationship with yourself is no longer contingent on how your body looks. When confidence is rooted in self-worth rather than appearance, your body no longer has to meet certain conditions before you allow yourself to participate in your own life.

item.title: What the World Cup Reveals About Human Nature
item.description:
Sport and Competition

What the World Cup Reveals About Human Nature

Why soccer taps into our ancient instincts for status, tribalism, and conflict.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • The World Cup activates ancient psychological systems for tribalism, status, and coalition-building.
  • Political leaders often use soccer victories for prestige but defeats can become political liabilities.
  • Soccer channels our evolved instincts for intergroup competition into a ritual—a substitute for conflict.

The FIFA World Cup is celebrated as a festival of sport, unity, and international friendship. Millions gather around screens, wear national colors, sing anthems, and ride the emotional roller coaster of hope, joy, outrage, and despair. Yet beneath the flags and fireworks lies something much older than soccer itself. The tournament taps into evolved psychological systems for status, coalition, and intergroup competition.

That is why politicians are so drawn to it. Soccer gives leaders access to something every politician wants but cannot easily manufacture: collective emotion. A winning team can make an entire nation feel stronger, more confident, and more united. Stand close enough to that success, and some of the glory may rub off.

Borrowing Glory

Psychologists have long known that people like to associate themselves with successful groups. After their university football team wins, students are more likely to say, “We won.” After a loss, they suddenly switch to “They lost.” This tendency is known as basking in reflected glory, or BIRGing.

It may sound trivial, but it reveals something fundamental about human psychology. Our identities are remarkably flexible. We expand our sense of self through successful groups, making their victories feel like our own.

Political leaders exploit exactly the same psychology. They do not need to score goals or lift trophies. They simply need to be photographed beside the winners. But the strategy comes with risks. Glory is contagious, but so is failure. A national defeat can quickly become a political embarrassment.

History offers many examples of leaders trying to turn sporting success into political capital—from Mussolini's 1934 World Cup to Putin's 2014 Winter Olympics. Although leaders may try to influence sporting events, they cannot fully script them. That uncertainty is precisely what makes sporting victories such powerful political symbols.

Why Soccer Feels Like War

From an evolutionary perspective, soccer is a remarkably realistic simulation of intergroup competition. Two coalitions compete for status before a public audience. There are clear group boundaries, visible symbols of identity, coordinated teamwork, and a public outcome that changes prestige. Although we consciously know it is “only a game,” older psychological systems often respond as though something deeply meaningful has happened to our group.

For some supporters, this becomes what psychologists call identity fusion: the team becomes part of the self. That helps explain why fans travel across continents, spend money they cannot really afford, and sometimes even fight over the outcome of a match.

This psychology reflects our evolutionary past. For most of human history, survival depended on belonging to cooperative groups that competed with rival groups over territory, resources, and status. Team sports tap into these ancient coalition-building instincts.

At the same time, sport serves an important social function. It channels competition into rituals governed by rules rather than violence. As George Orwell famously observed, soccer is “war minus the shooting.” The stadium is not a battlefield, but neither is it psychologically neutral.

Expanding the Tribe

Yet the same psychology that divides the world into “us” and “them” can also expand the boundaries of “us.”

During this year's World Cup, tens of thousands of Dutch supporters transformed Kansas City, Dallas, and Houston into seas of orange. What was striking was not only the spectacle itself, but how many Americans enthusiastically joined the celebrations, wearing orange shirts, learning Dutch chants, and cheering for the Netherlands as honorary members of the Orange Army.

From an evolutionary perspective, this is just as interesting as fierce rivalry. Humans are remarkably flexible in forming new alliances. Under the right conditions, strangers can quickly become teammates. The World Cup does not simply create enemies; it also creates temporary coalitions that cross national boundaries.

When Games Become Political

The darker side appears when collective status is threatened. A controversial referee decision can feel like injustice. A painful defeat can feel like national humiliation. Sport rarely causes political conflict by itself, but it can amplify tensions that already exist.

The 1969 Football War between Honduras and El Salvador remains the classic example. The underlying causes were political and economic, but World Cup qualifying matches became the emotional trigger that transformed existing grievances into open conflict.

We did not have to wait long for an illustration during this World Cup. Following South Korea's unexpected exit from the 2026 World Cup, President Lee Jae Myung publicly declared himself “utterly baffled” by the team's performance, criticized the national coach, questioned personnel decisions, and ordered a government investigation. Within hours, the coach resigned. The reaction was about far more than tactics. Sporting defeats often become symbolic defeats for the nation—and, by extension, for those who lead it.

This helps explain why political leaders appear in locker rooms, wrap themselves in national flags, and celebrate alongside victorious athletes. They are not merely enjoying the spectacle. They are participating in an ancient status ritual that links their own reputation to the fortunes of the group.

Civilization's Greatest Team Sport

There is, however, reason for optimism.

The World Cup demonstrates that human rivalry can be civilized. We evolved to care deeply about status, coalition, and group identity. Those tendencies have not disappeared. Instead, institutions such as sport provide rules, referees, rituals, and shared norms that allow intense competition without widespread violence.

A Middle East Cup including Israel, Palestine, Lebanon, Iran, and Iraq would not solve the region’s conflicts. Of course not. But as a symbol, it would matter. It would say that rivals can confront one another without destroying one another. In human affairs, that is already progress.

Perhaps civilization works not by eliminating human nature, but by giving it better outlets.

The World Cup reminds us that humans did not evolve as isolated individuals. We evolved to belong to teams, compete with rival groups, and celebrate collective victories. Soccer activates these ancient psychological systems. That is why politicians seek to borrow its glory, victories feel intensely personal, and defeats resonate far beyond the final whistle.

The game has changed over thousands of years. The psychology behind it has not.

Many of the ideas discussed here are explored in greater depth in FC Sapiens: What Football Tells Us About Human Nature (international edition: Bloomsbury, 2027).

item.title: Why AI Feels Human and Even Conscious
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why AI Feels Human and Even Conscious

How AI can sound human by linking ideas like our minds do, without actual consciousness.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI predicts language by finding patterns and associations.
  • Large Language Models connect ideas that resemble human conversations.
  • This associative flow makes AI responses feel surprisingly natural.
Source: Stock-Asso/Shutterstock

For over a century, the heart of psychoanalysis has been free association—the practice of suspending censorship and allowing the mind to wander, revealing the hidden patterns of the unconscious.¹ Today, a parallel has emerged in the digital world of artificial intelligence.

AI uses a modern Large Language Model (LLM), but it doesn't simply retrieve facts from a database. Instead, it navigates a vast network of probabilities, predicting each successive fact or word based on patterns learned from the annals of human language.

Recent research suggests that large language models function much like associative memory systems, retrieving information through contextual relationships rather than simple storage retrieval and lookup.² The result is an associative flow that often feels remarkably human, echoing the way our minds connect ideas, thoughts, metaphors, and memories. This raises a profound question: if the human unconscious is, as Lacan has said, structured like a language,³ and AI is fundamentally an engine of language, does artificial intelligence mirror the structure of the unconscious?

Why AI Sounds Like a Mind at Work

To answer this question, we must first distinguish between a machine and a person. In psychoanalytic theory, the unconscious is a vast warehouse of repressed wishes, fears, and memories. Freud believed that unconscious material reveals itself indirectly through dreams, slips of the tongue, and symbolic narratives.⁴ Further, Lacan expanded this idea, arguing that the unconscious, itself, operates through a chain link of signifiers, metaphors, and linguistic associations.⁵

But artificial intelligence has no childhood, no trauma, and no personal memories. It has no repressed thoughts because it has no psyche to repress them. While AI can generate language that resembles human thought, it possesses no inner life from which those thoughts emerge. Yet its inner workings, particularly a mechanism known as self-attention, bear a striking resemblance to aspects of human associative thinking... the way we connect ideas to other ideas without step-by-step logic.

With regard to AI, self-attention is the mechanism that allows it to decide which words in a sentence matter most when understanding or generating the next word. It's one of the reasons AI can produce responses that feel real as well as associative in texture.⁶ Just as our minds link ideas across the narrative landscape of our lived experience, AI maps an immense network of relationships drawn from humanity's collective written record, producing a digital reflection of how we express our inner lives.

Researchers have even found that although AI does not think or feel as human beings do, it can reproduce linguistic patterns that resemble the associative dynamics revealed through free association.⁷ Similarly, it's vital to realize that human free association arises from an inner subjective life filled with emotions, conflict, thoughts, and memories. And that artificial intelligence emerges from statistics, probability, and pattern recognition. One speaks from the unconscious; the other speaks from a digital architecture of association.

Perhaps this is why AI feels so uncannily human. It doesn't possess an unconscious mind, but it mirrors the associative pathways through which our own minds generate meaning. In doing so, artificial intelligence becomes less of a manufactured kind of psyche but more of a sophisticated mirror—reflecting back to us the meaningful structures of language that shape our own thoughts.

item.title: How to Do Special Time With Your Child, Even When It Seems Hard
item.description:
Parenting

How to Do Special Time With Your Child, Even When It Seems Hard

What to do during Special Time with your child—and how to stay present if struggling.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Putting your phone in another room, not just face-down, signals to your child that this time is theirs.
  • Letting your child lead during Special Time also meets their need for autonomy, reducing power struggles.
  • A child who hears yes during Special Time is more likely to accept a no from you when it really counts.

In Part 1, we looked at why children show attention-seeking behavior—and why the most effective response isn't a firmer boundary, but a more consistent source of connection. Special Time is that source: a short, daily block of one-on-one time where your child leads and you follow, phone out of the room, full attention on them. Ten minutes a day, done consistently, meets the need that's been driving the behavior.

But knowing what Special Time is and actually doing it well are two different things. Here's what makes the difference.

How Do I Build a Better Relationship With My Child?

Special Time works because it targets something specific: your child's need for connection with you. But there's a difference between spending time together and spending time in a way that actually meets that need. These five practices make the difference.

  1. Put your phone in another room. Not face-down on the table. Actually out of the room. Even a quick glance at a notification pulls you out of the present moment—and your child notices. A phone on the table, even a silent one, signals that they're competing for your attention. This is their time.

  2. Let them lead. Ask what they want to do. If they don't know, suggest something they often ask for, or something they always say yes to. Adults control most of what children do all day. Special Time also addresses a child's need for autonomy—and when that need gets met consistently, they spend less of the rest of the day trying to wrestle control back from you.

  3. Say yes as much as you can. If they want a pillow fight and you're exhausted, you don't have to do the full 10 minutes of pillow fight. Two minutes counts. Then you could suggest a dance party. The goal is to make yes your default when it's safe to do so. A child who hears yes during Special Time learns that their preferences matter to you—and that makes them more willing to accept a no when it really counts.

  4. Keep it one-on-one. Special Time is just you and the child whose turn it is. Other kids, your partner, your to-do list—they can all wait 10 minutes. If you have multiple children, each one gets their own separate Special Time. When your child knows this time belongs to them alone, it sends a clear signal: You are important to me.

  5. Make it predictable. If your child never knows whether Special Time will happen or whether it will get cut short, they'll keep finding other ways to make sure their need for connection gets met. Consistency is what makes this work. Weeks later, if you're frustrated with your child's behavior, there's a good chance you'll realize you've let Special Time slide—and that's the moment to bring it back.

What if You Struggle to Connect With Your Child?

One parent, Aija, came to one of our Beyond the Behavior coaching calls with exactly this problem. Her son was 4 and a half. No matter how much time she spent with him, it never seemed like enough. She'd play and play, and he'd still be asking for more. She started dreading the moment she stepped out of the bedroom in the morning and heard "Let's play."

When we dug into it, we found something underneath the frustration: messages Aija had absorbed growing up—that productivity was valuable, and play was a waste of time. Every time she sat down with her son, her brain was telling her she should be doing something more useful. Those messages were still running in the background. Every time she sat down to play with him, her brain was telling her she should be doing something more productive.

If that's familiar, a few things helped Aija—and many other parents:

  1. Offer activities you enjoy first. Aija liked building Legos and painting. Her son did, too. When you offer activities you enjoy as the first option, you're more likely to find something you both like—and you'll be more present during it.

  2. Use Special Time as a mindfulness practice. When your mind wanders to the chores or the thought that you're wasting time, don't fight it. Acknowledge it: "I'm thinking I should be doing laundry right now." Then come back to what's in front of you. When my daughter was 5, she wanted to sort gravel by color every single day during Special Time. Not exactly riveting. But when I reminded myself that the real point of the activity was to connect with her, and that the actual experience of it was not terrible, I could be present and enjoy it with her. It's only 10 minutes.

  3. Start with just two minutes. If 10 minutes feels overwhelming, start with two. Sit on the floor with them. Follow their lead. Many parents find that once they're in it, the resistance beforehand was harder than the thing itself.

  4. Let go of the outcome. Special Time doesn't have to look meaningful to be meaningful. Your child doesn't need you to be enthusiastic. They need you to be there. Showing up consistently—even when you're not fully into it—still meets their need for connection.

  5. No high-stakes activities. This is not the time for a Pinterest-perfect activity that takes longer to set up and clean up than your child plays with it. Simple is great.

  6. Try to avoid screen time if you can. But if you have a child you’re struggling to connect with, and they are really into a screen activity, start by having them tell and/or teach you about it. That creates an opening to branch out into a nonscreen activity in a few days/weeks.

  7. Notice what changes. If you're struggling to stay motivated, track your child's behavior for a few days before you start, then again after a week of Special Time. Many parents see dramatic shifts the very same day they begin.

Final Thoughts

When your child's need for connection is met consistently, attention-seeking behavior tends to fade on its own. Not because you've managed it—but because the thing driving it is no longer there.

A predictable 10 minutes of one-on-one time, with your child choosing the activity. It's a small change in your day. It can be a significant change in your parenting relationship.
